interactions.summary: Jiang closes the free-will choice from Paradise 6, then pivots to the theological puzzle he wants Beatrice to solve: why Jesus had to sacrifice himself at all.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang framing the next theological problem

interactions.summary: A student suggests Jesus dies and rises to prove he is the true son of God, and Jiang notes that some Christian denominations teach that demonstration model.

Another student argues that sacrificing one's son is the highest possible representation of love; Jiang presses whether Jesus really remained sacrificed and says this love framing is close to Dante's own explanation.

A student objects that resurrection would turn faith into fact and argues that Jesus freely chose self-sacrifice rather than being sacrificed by God; Jiang accepts that correction while preserving the claim that Jesus and God are one.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student philosophical objection with Jiang acceptance

interactions.summary: A student reads Beatrice's entrance and the sentence that names Dante's problem directly: how just vengeance can itself deserve just punishment.

claims.claim: Jiang says the free-will choice from the Justinian canto leads directly into Dante's next question: why Jesus had to sacrifice himself at all if salvation is supposed to restore justice.
A live student answer proposes that Jesus dies and resurrects in order to prove he is truly divine, and Jiang says some denominations in fact teach the crucifixion-resurrection this way.
claims.temporal_scope: Classroom answer and Jiang acknowledgement on 2026-06-16.

claims.claim: A second classroom answer says the willingness to sacrifice one's son is the largest possible representation of divine love, and Jiang says that love logic is close to Dante's explanation.

A student argument Jiang endorses says resurrection cannot simply function as proof without collapsing faith into fact, and that the cleaner framing is that Jesus chooses self-sacrifice through free will.
Jiang retains the Trinitarian compression that Jesus and God are the same thing even after conceding that Jesus, not God as an external actor, chooses the sacrifice.
The Dante passage Jiang assigns names the governing paradox as a justice problem: how divine vengeance against sin can itself call for another just punishment.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang states the crucifixion problem in blunt modern language instead of pious abstraction.
signature_moments.source_phrase: tell me exactly why jesus had to kill himself
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves the packet's pressure point: Dante's theology only matters if it can survive a hard question about why sacrifice was needed at all.

signature_moments.moment: A student flips the whole proving-divinity model by arguing that visible resurrection would erase faith and that sacrifice has to remain a free choice.
signature_moments.source_phrase: that's not faith anymore is it that's just i saw him rise from the dead it's a fact
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the sharpest classroom intervention in the packet and gives Jiang a cleaner free-will framing for the crucifixion.

signature_moments.moment: Beatrice's problem arrives as a knot of justice: just vengeance somehow becoming the ground of another just punishment.
signature_moments.source_phrase: how just vengeance can deserve just punishment
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It names the formal paradox that the next packets will spend time untangling.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Beatrice's term for God's rightful anger at human sin, which then raises the puzzle of why redemption still requires punishment.
The student and Jiang's preferred framing that Jesus freely chooses the cross rather than being passively offered up by another agent.
The distinction a student uses to argue that obvious empirical proof of resurrection would undermine the very structure of belief.

chronology_notes.note: This 2026-06-16 packet marks the live class pivot from Paradise 6's free-will moral choice into Beatrice's later theological explanation of why crucifixion becomes the path of redemption.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang says the love-through-sacrifice answer is 'Dante's explanation as well,' but the packet only supports that as a live interpretive alignment, not as a precise doctrinal summary of every line in the canto.
